valueChain.summary: Logistics firms charge shippers per parcel, kilogram, trip or square foot, then make money by filling trucks, hubs, warehouses and riders as densely as possible, because most of their cost is tied to capacity rather than to each shipment. Outside dense networks and contracted warehousing margins are thin, so small changes in utilisation, empty running or failed deliveries swing profit.

stages.name: Sales, pricing and booking
activities: Win and contract shippers (marketplaces, D2C brands, manufacturers)
Set rate cards by weight slab and zone and negotiate discounts
Integrate shippers' order systems and generate labels and manifests
Match loads to trucks (freight brokers)
players: Express and PTL carriers' sales teams
Shipping aggregators reselling several carriers to small sellers
Freight brokers and digital freight marketplaces
revenueDrivers: Rate per shipment, kg or trip by zone and weight
Broker take rate on freight value
costDrivers: Discounts and rebates to large clients

kpis.name: Yield per shipment
kpis.benchmark: about ₹65-80 for Indian B2C express parcels (approx.)

kpis.name: Top-10 client share
kpis.formula: revenue from top 10 clients / total revenue
kpis.benchmark: can exceed 40% for express carriers that depend on marketplaces (approx.)

stages.marginNote: Earns little on its own but sets the price of everything downstream; asset-light freight brokers keep roughly 5-10% of freight value as gross margin (approx.).

stages.name: First-mile pickup
activities: Schedule pickups from seller warehouses, factories and stores
Collect parcels or consignments by bike, van or small truck
Scan and check weight and dimensions at pickup
Bring loads to the origin hub
players: Franchise and channel partners in smaller towns
Shippers dropping off at carrier counters
revenueDrivers: Usually bundled into the shipment rate
Pickup fees for small or ad hoc shippers
costDrivers: Wasted visits when nothing is ready

kpis.name: Pickup success rate
kpis.formula: pickups completed on the scheduled day / pickups scheduled

kpis.name: Pickup cost per parcel
kpis.benchmark: roughly ₹4-8 for dense metro sellers, far higher for low-volume sellers (approx.)

stages.marginNote: A cost centre, typically 5-10% of network cost per parcel (approx.); its economics swing on pickup density.

stages.name: Hub sorting and warehousing
activities: Receive, scan and sort parcels by destination at origin hubs
Consolidate bags and pallets for line haul
Store, pick and pack client inventory in fulfilment centres
Cross-dock part-truckload consignments
revenueDrivers: Storage fees per sq ft or pallet
Handling fees per unit and value-added services (kitting, labelling)
For express carriers, bundled into the shipment rate

kpis.name: Mis-sort rate
kpis.formula: parcels sent to the wrong destination / parcels sorted

kpis.name: Warehouse space utilisation
kpis.formula: occupied pallet positions / available pallet positions

stages.marginNote: Contract warehousing earns roughly 8-12% EBITDA on multi-year contracts (approx.); express sortation is a cost centre where automation pays only at high volume.

stages.name: Line haul
activities: Move consolidated loads between hubs by road, rail or air
Plan departures to meet hub cut-off times
Find return loads to cut empty running
Track trucks and manage drivers
players: Small fleet owners (a few trucks each)
Air cargo and rail container operators
revenueDrivers: Freight per trip, tonne or km (FTL)
costDrivers: Diesel (roughly half of truck running cost, approx.)

kpis.name: Empty running share
kpis.benchmark: commonly cited at about 25-40% of truck km in India; estimates vary widely by source and segment (approx.)

kpis.name: Truck fill rate
kpis.formula: load carried / truck capacity (weight or volume)
kpis.benchmark: 80-90% targeted on scheduled express and PTL lanes (approx.)

stages.marginNote: Thin for small fleet owners (low single-digit net margin, approx.); scale, return loads and fill rate separate winners from losers.

stages.name: Last-mile delivery
activities: Sort parcels by route at destination delivery centres
Assign routes to riders
Attempt delivery, collect COD cash and record proof of delivery
Reattempt or mark for return after failed attempts
players: Carriers' delivery centres and riders (often contract or gig staff)
Franchise delivery partners in small towns
revenueDrivers: Premiums for same-day or time-slot delivery
costDrivers: Failed attempts and low drop density

kpis.name: First-attempt delivery success
kpis.formula: parcels delivered on first attempt / parcels out for delivery
kpis.benchmark: about 85-90% in metros, lower for COD and small towns (approx.)

stages.marginNote: The largest single cost, often 35-45% of network cost per parcel (approx.); drop density decides profit.

stages.name: Returns, COD and claims
activities: Return undelivered parcels to sellers (RTO) and run reverse pickups
Remit COD cash to shippers
Settle claims for lost or damaged shipments
Reconcile invoices and weight disputes
players: Carriers' reverse logistics and finance teams
Banks and payment partners handling COD remittance
revenueDrivers: COD handling fees (flat or % of COD value)
costDrivers: Reverse line haul and handling of RTO parcels
Compensation for lost and damaged parcels

kpis.name: RTO rate
kpis.formula: parcels returned to origin / parcels dispatched
kpis.benchmark: roughly 20-30% on COD orders (industry data for FY25 put it near 26%) against under 2-3% on prepaid (approx.)

kpis.name: COD remittance cycle
kpis.formula: days from delivery to cash credited to the shipper
kpis.benchmark: about D+2 to D+7 when booked directly with Indian express carriers; faster paid options exist (approx.)

stages.marginNote: Mostly a cost and cash stage: RTO is close to pure loss, while COD collections give the carrier a few days of interest-free float.

valueChain.profitPools: Profit concentrates where density and contracts lock in volume: large express and PTL networks with well-utilised hubs and lanes, contract warehousing on multi-year deals, and asset-light brokers that keep a margin without owning trucks. Small truck owners in line haul and contract riders in last mile earn the least, because their capacity is a commodity and pricing power sits with shippers and the networks that aggregate them.

unitEconomics.unit: per B2C express parcel at a mid-sized Indian carrier (approx.)

lines.item: Revenue per parcel (base freight plus surcharges)
RTO cost not recovered from shippers
COD cash handling and payment costs

unitEconomics.result: Contribution per parcel ≈ ₹7 (about 9% of revenue), before roughly ₹4-5 of technology and corporate overheads; the scale leader runs several points higher because denser routes cut last-mile and line haul cost per parcel

valueChain.india: Road carries roughly 65-70% of India's freight, and trucking is highly fragmented, with most trucks owned by operators running fewer than five vehicles. GST (2017) and e-way bills removed state check posts and let shippers consolidate into fewer, larger warehouses, while the National Logistics Policy (2022), PM Gati Shakti and the dedicated freight corridors aim to cut logistics costs, which the first official estimate (NCAER for DPIIT, 2025) put at about 8% of GDP for 2023-24, well below the 13-14% long quoted. E-commerce delivery is shaped by a high share of cash-on-delivery orders, which drives RTO rates and COD remittance economics.

workedExample.problem: An express carrier's contribution per parcel fell about ₹3.5 (roughly 5 points of revenue) over two quarters, with its rate card unchanged.
trace: Revenue per parcel is flat (same rate card, same zone mix by distance), so the fall is on the cost side; walk the chain stage by stage.
First-mile, hub and line haul cost per parcel are flat; last-mile cost per parcel is up about ₹3.5.
Rider pay per day is unchanged at about ₹750, but the share of parcels going to Tier-3 towns rose from 20% to 45% after new marketplace clients were signed.
Tier-3 riders make about 20 drops a day against 32 in metros, so cost per drop is ~₹37.5 against ~₹23.4; a 25-point mix shift adds ~₹3.5 per parcel on average.
The root cause sits in pricing and booking: the zonal rate card prices by distance, not by delivery density, so Tier-3 parcels in the same zone are priced like metro parcels.
workedExample.lesson: Costs often surface in last mile, but the fix may sit upstream in how contracts and rate cards are priced.

cases.title: Truck fleet's profit falls on flat revenue
cases.prompt: Our client is a Ludhiana-based full-truckload transporter with 120 trucks, mostly carrying goods for North Indian manufacturers. Revenue has stayed flat at about ₹55 crore for two years, but profit before tax has fallen from ₹4 crore to ₹1.2 crore. What is driving the decline?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Find the cause and get profit before tax back to about ₹4 crore within a year.
Q: Has the fleet changed? A: Still 120 trucks, no new purchases in three years, so average truck age has gone from about 3 to 5 years.
Q: How much do the trucks run? A: Total km per truck has risen from about 9,500 to 10,000 a month; the client has not tracked how much of that is loaded versus empty.

Q: Anything changed with customers or costs? A: A Gujarat client that gave return loads was lost last year, and rates on the remaining forward contracts rose slightly; diesel prices have been broadly flat.

modelTree.label: Why has PBT fallen from ₹4 crore to ₹1.2 crore on flat revenue?

children.label: Revenue (trucks x loaded km x rate)
Driver trip allowances and en-route expenses
Depreciation and interest on truck loans

hypotheses: Since the Gujarat client left, trucks run about 500 extra empty km a month to reach their next load, lifting empty running from about 25% to 30%; at roughly ₹30 of variable cost per km (diesel, tolls, tyres, allowances) that adds about ₹2.2 crore a year (120 trucks x 500 km x 12 x ₹30), while slightly higher forward rates hold revenue flat on about 2% fewer loaded km.

Ageing from 3 to 5 years has raised tyre and repair cost by about ₹0.5 per km, roughly ₹0.7 crore a year on 1.44 crore km; with the extra empty km this explains almost all of the ₹2.8 crore fall, so fixed costs need only a check.
hints: Use the profit equation, and split costs by what they move with.
First level: Revenue, Variable costs (per km run), Fixed costs (per truck).
Fixed costs per truck: depreciation and interest on truck loans, driver salaries, insurance, permits and road tax, office and admin overheads.

keyMetrics.name: Empty running share
keyMetrics.formula: empty km / total km

keyMetrics.name: Cost per loaded km
keyMetrics.formula: total operating cost / loaded km

commonMistakes: Concluding from flat revenue and flat diesel prices that operations have not changed, when total km rose while loaded km fell.
Treating diesel and tolls as tied to revenue rather than to km run, which hides the cost of empty repositioning.

frameworkPick.why: The question is why profit fell while revenue held, so the first job is to split profit into revenue and cost drivers and find which moved.

distractorWhyNot.operations: Fleet operations may well be the root cause, but the question is about profit, and operations is one branch inside the cost side, not the starting structure.
distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: Nothing needs sizing; the client's own revenue and profit are known.
distractorWhyNot.turnaround: The firm is still profitable and has no cash crisis, so jumping to a restructuring plan skips the diagnosis.

cases.title: Sizing India's e-commerce parcel delivery market
cases.prompt: A global logistics investor is studying India's e-commerce delivery sector. Assume about 250 million Indians shop online. How large is the annual revenue pool for delivering e-commerce parcels in India, including returns?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Which shipments count? A: All B2C e-commerce parcels delivered to consumers, whether by third-party carriers or marketplaces' own fleets; exclude food delivery and quick commerce.
Q: What is 'revenue'? A: What shippers pay for delivery (or the cost captive fleets incur), not the value of the goods, for the current year.
Q: How often do people order? A: Assume about 16 orders per online shopper per year, one parcel per order.

Q: Prices and returns? A: Assume about ₹65 per forward parcel; returns (customer returns plus RTO) are about 15% of forward parcels at about ₹60 each, lower on marketplaces and far higher on COD-heavy D2C.

modelTree.label: Annual revenue from delivering e-commerce parcels in India (₹ crore)

children.label: Mix of parcels by zone (intra-city, regional, national)
Rate per parcel in each zone

hypotheses: Forward deliveries make up nearly 90% of the pool (roughly 4 billion parcels x ₹65 ≈ ₹26,000 crore), so the answer is most sensitive to orders per shopper and the average rate.

Returns add roughly ₹3,600 crore (about 60 crore parcels x ₹60), taking the pool to about ₹30,000 crore; fashion-heavy and COD-heavy D2C shippers carry a far larger returns share than this blended 15%.
hints: Split by direction of the parcel, then use volume x price within each part.
First level: Forward delivery revenue and Return delivery revenue.
Return delivery revenue: number of return parcels (customer returns, RTO) x average revenue per return parcel (price per reverse pickup, price per RTO parcel).

keyMetrics.name: Delivery revenue pool
keyMetrics.formula: forward parcels x revenue per forward parcel + return parcels x revenue per return parcel

commonMistakes: Taking e-commerce GMV and applying a percentage without a shipment count, which gives no way to sanity-check the answer.
Forgetting returns and RTO, or counting RTO parcels both as forward deliveries and again as returns at the full forward rate.

frameworkPick.why: The question asks how big an annual revenue pool is, which needs a volume x price estimate built from shoppers, orders and rates.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The investor may later decide whether to enter, but the question asked is only the size of the pool.
distractorWhyNot.growth: There is no client trying to grow revenue; the task is to estimate today's market.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Splitting by zone or return type is a step inside the estimate, not the purpose of the question.

cases.title: Cutting cost at a costly delivery centre
cases.prompt: Our client, a large Indian express parcel carrier, runs about 2,500 delivery centres. Its centre in Hinjewadi, Pune delivers about 6,000 parcels a day at ₹36 per delivered parcel, against ₹27 at comparable Pune centres. How would you bring the cost down?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the target? A: About ₹28 per delivered parcel within six months, without hurting delivery success or customer complaints.
Q: How are riders used? A: About 210 riders a day at roughly ₹950 per rider-day including fuel; they average about 29 successful deliveries each against about 40 at peer centres.
Q: Delivery success? A: First-attempt success is 78% against 89% at peers; COD is 55% of parcels against 45% at peers.
Q: Anything special about the area? A: Mostly IT offices and large gated societies; residents are away by day and gate entry checks take 5-10 minutes per visit.

modelTree.label: How can Hinjewadi cut cost per delivered parcel from ₹36 to ~₹28?

children.label: Pay structure (fixed day rate vs per-delivery incentive)
Time per stop (gate entry, OTP, cash)
Customer away (time slots, society desk drop)

hypotheses: Low first-attempt success (78% vs 89%) means about 14% more attempts per delivered parcel, mostly from residents being away by day; time-slot delivery and drops at society desks would recover most of it.
Gate entry checks of 5-10 minutes cap attempts at about 37 per rider-day against about 45 at peers; pre-registered rider access or society-level consolidated drops would lift it.
hints: Write cost per delivered parcel as an equation and split along its terms.
First level: Rider cost per rider-day, Successful deliveries per rider-day, Centre overheads per delivered parcel.
Rider cost per rider-day: pay structure (fixed day rate vs per-delivery incentive) and fuel and vehicle allowance.

keyMetrics.name: Cost per delivered parcel
keyMetrics.formula: rider cost per rider-day / successful deliveries per rider-day + centre overheads / parcels delivered

keyMetrics.name: First-attempt success rate
keyMetrics.formula: parcels delivered on first attempt / parcels out for delivery

commonMistakes: Going straight to cutting rider pay, when the gap is productivity (29 vs 40 deliveries) and lower pay would raise attrition and failed attempts.
Measuring productivity on attempts rather than successful deliveries, which hides the cost of failed attempts.

frameworkPick.why: The question is how to lower a unit cost at one site against peer benchmarks, which is a process and productivity problem.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: Revenue is not in question; the gap is one cost line at one centre, so a full revenue and cost tree wastes half the structure.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: Charging shippers more for this area does not reduce the cost of delivery, which is what was asked.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Adding volume might improve density, but the question is about cutting cost on the current volume.

cases.title: Pricing same-day delivery in London
cases.prompt: A mid-sized UK parcel carrier is launching same-day delivery in Greater London for online retailers, for orders placed by noon. Its standard next-day service costs retailers about £3.50 a parcel. What price should it charge retailers for same-day?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Profitable within 18 months, targeting about 20,000 same-day parcels a day by year two.

Q: What does it cost? A: Incremental cost is estimated at £5.50-6.50 per parcel at 20,000 a day (dedicated vans running two waves, lower drop density), plus about £4 million a year of fixed costs for a dedicated hub and software.
Q: What do alternatives charge? A: Specialist same-day couriers charge retailers about £7-10 a parcel; some large retailers run their own vans.
Q: What do retailers gain? A: Fashion and electronics retailers report higher conversion when same-day is offered, and many charge shoppers £5-7 for it.

modelTree.label: What per-parcel price should the carrier charge retailers for London same-day?

children.label: Incremental cost per parcel (collection, hub, van and driver)
Fixed launch costs per parcel at target volume
Fee retailers can charge shoppers for same-day

hypotheses: A price of about £7 per parcel covers incremental cost of ~£6 and, at 20,000 parcels a day over ~300 trading days, earns about £6 million of contribution against £4 million of fixed costs, while sitting at the bottom of the specialist couriers' £7-10 range.
Retailers' value ceiling is about £8-9 per parcel (the £5-7 they charge shoppers plus some conversion gain), so pricing near specialists' top end would limit uptake to large premium retailers.
hints: Bound the range the price can sit in first, then decide where in that range to sit.
First level: Cost floor, Value to retailers (ceiling), Competing alternatives.
Competing alternatives: specialist same-day couriers (£7-10), gig-economy delivery platforms, and retailers' own vans and click-and-collect.

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per parcel
keyMetrics.formula: price - incremental cost per parcel

keyMetrics.name: Break-even volume
keyMetrics.formula: annual fixed launch costs / contribution per parcel

commonMistakes: Pricing as a mark-up on the £3.50 next-day rate, ignoring that same-day has a different cost base and a different value to retailers.
Treating cost per parcel as fixed, when it depends heavily on volume and drop density; price and volume must be set together.

frameworkPick.why: The launch decision is made and the question is the price, so cost floor, customer value and competitor reference points are the right structure.

distractorWhyNot.product-launch: Whether and how to launch is already decided; a launch framework spends time on readiness and go-to-market that was not asked.
distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The carrier already operates in London parcels; this is a new service in its existing market, and the question is price.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: There is no existing profit problem to diagnose; cost is one input to the price decision.

cases.title: Doubling a part-truckload network's revenue
cases.prompt: Our client is a national part-truckload (PTL) freight company moving B2B consignments for manufacturers and distributors through 25 hubs. Revenue is ₹1,800 crore, growing 8% a year while the PTL market grows about 12%. The board wants to double revenue in five years. How should it get there?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Any profit constraint? A: EBITDA margin, now about 11%, must not fall below 10%.
Q: Customer mix? A: About 60% of revenue from 400 enterprise accounts and 40% from about 25,000 SMEs booked through branch franchisees.

Q: Why is it growing slower than the market? A: It has lost share in auto components and in marketplace-to-seller replenishment, where rivals offer 2-3 day express PTL against its 4-5 days; tonnage per enterprise account is flat.
Q: Are acquisitions allowed? A: Yes, up to ₹500 crore, but the board prefers organic growth first.

modelTree.label: How can revenue double to ₹3,600 crore in five years (~15% a year)?

children.label: Higher share on lanes already served (faster transit)
Lanes and plants not yet served
Rate increases and fuel surcharge pass-through
Wider franchise coverage in Tier-2/3 towns
Build near existing hubs for current accounts

hypotheses: Growing core PTL at the market's 12% gets to only about ₹3,170 crore in five years, so roughly ₹430 crore must come from adjacencies or above-market share gains.
Share loss in auto components comes from 4-5 day transit against 2-3 days for rivals; a time-definite express PTL product could add 2-3 points of annual growth from existing accounts.
Contract warehousing sold to the 400 enterprise accounts is the fastest adjacency and lifts margin, while FTL brokerage adds revenue at low margin and must be capped to protect the 10% EBITDA floor.
hints: Use an Ansoff-style split on who you sell to and what you sell them.
First level: Core PTL with existing customers, Core PTL with new customers, Adjacent services.
Core PTL with new customers: new enterprise accounts (pharma, electronics, auto aftermarket and others) and more SME shippers (franchise coverage in Tier-2/3 towns, digital self-booking).

keyMetrics.name: PTL revenue
keyMetrics.formula: tonnage x yield per kg

keyMetrics.name: Required CAGR
keyMetrics.formula: (target revenue / current revenue)^(1/years) - 1 = 2^(1/5) - 1 ≈ 14.9%

commonMistakes: Listing initiatives without sizing whether together they close the ₹1,800 crore gap in five years.
Ignoring the 10% EBITDA floor, for example buying volume with price cuts or piling into low-margin brokerage.

frameworkPick.why: The board wants a revenue target reached, so the structure should lay out every source of growth (existing customers, new customers, new services) and size each.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: Entering warehousing is one option inside the plan, not the question itself.
distractorWhyNot.ma: Acquisitions are allowed but the board prefers organic growth; a deal is one lever, not the frame.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: Margins are healthy at 11%; the problem is slow growth, with margin only a constraint.

cases.title: Should a 3PL enter cold chain?
cases.prompt: Our client is an Indian contract logistics company running 8 million sq ft of ambient warehouses for FMCG and retail clients, with revenue of ₹1,100 crore. It is considering entering temperature-controlled warehousing for pharma and food. Should it, and if so how?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does success look like? A: A business line of ₹300 crore revenue in five years at 15%+ EBITDA, against about 9% in ambient warehousing.
Q: How much can it invest? A: Up to ₹600 crore; temperature-controlled space costs roughly 3-4 times as much to build per pallet position as ambient.

Q: What does the market look like? A: Highly fragmented; most cold storage capacity is single-commodity potato stores in UP and West Bengal, while modern multi-temperature capacity near metros is scarce.

Q: What does the client bring? A: No temperature-controlled experience, but strong relationships with FMCG companies whose dairy, frozen and ice cream lines are growing, and a proven warehouse management system.

modelTree.label: Should the client enter temperature-controlled warehousing, and how?

children.label: Rent and service premium over ambient
Captive cold chains of pharma and dairy firms
FMCG clients with dairy and frozen lines
Warehouse system and sites near metros
Partner with a cold chain operator

hypotheses: Modern pharma and processed-food capacity near metros is scarce enough to earn 15%+ EBITDA, unlike oversupplied potato cold stores that set misleadingly low average rents.
Acquiring or partnering with a specialist beats greenfield, because pharma clients require an audited compliance track record that takes 2-3 years to build.
Food cold chain for existing FMCG clients can be entered organically within the ₹600 crore budget, giving a base-load tenant before pharma.
hints: Use the standard entry questions, working from the market inwards to the client and ending with the money and the route in.
First level: Market attractiveness, Competitive landscape, Client's ability to win, Economics and entry mode.

Client's ability to win: transferable strengths (FMCG clients with dairy and frozen lines, warehouse system and metro sites) and capability gaps (refrigeration engineering and energy management, pharma compliance).

keyMetrics.name: Payback per pallet position
keyMetrics.formula: build capex per pallet / (annual revenue per pallet - annual operating cost per pallet)

keyMetrics.name: Utilisation
keyMetrics.formula: occupied pallet positions / available pallet positions

commonMistakes: Sizing the market from total cold storage capacity, which is dominated by potato stores, instead of the addressable modern pharma and food segment.
Assuming ambient warehousing skills transfer, ignoring refrigeration engineering, power management and pharma compliance.

frameworkPick.why: The client must decide whether to move into a new segment needing new capabilities and capital, so attractiveness, competition, ability to win and entry mode are the right lenses.

distractorWhyNot.growth: Cold chain is one specific growth option; the question is a yes or no on that segment, not how to grow overall.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: This is not an extension of an existing service to current customers; it needs new assets, skills and regulatory compliance, which entry analysis covers.
distractorWhyNot.ma: Acquisition is one possible entry mode, assessed inside the market entry structure.

cases.title: Responding to a funded rival's price cuts
cases.prompt: Our client is one of India's three largest B2C express parcel carriers, with revenue of ₹4,000 crore. A newly funded rival is offering D2C brands rates about 20% below the client's, plus next-day COD remittance. D2C brands contribute 25% of the client's revenue. How should the client respond?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Protect D2C share and profit over the next two years.
Q: What has been lost so far? A: About 6% of D2C volume moved to the rival last quarter, mostly small brands shipping under 500 parcels a day.
Q: What do we know about the rival? A: It raised about ₹600 crore last year and covers about 8,000 pin codes against the client's 18,000.
Q: Client's D2C economics? A: Contribution margin of about 12% on D2C against 8% on marketplace volume; D2C COD collections average about ₹20 crore a day and are remitted weekly (D+7).

modelTree.label: How should the client respond to a funded rival undercutting D2C rates by 20%?

children.label: How serious and lasting is the threat
Which D2C customers are at risk
Large brands (value coverage, integrations, low RTO)
Can the rival sustain the price
Rival's cost per parcel vs its price
What is at stake for the client
Volume likely to switch, by segment
Knock-on cost from lower density on shared routes
Selective rate cuts for at-risk large brands
Coverage in pin codes the rival lacks

hypotheses: An across-the-board 20% match would cost about ₹200 crore of D2C revenue, more than the segment's entire ~₹120 crore contribution, so any price response must be selective.

Large brands care more about remittance speed and coverage than price; moving from D+7 to D+2 means funding five days of COD collections (about ₹100 crore), roughly ₹10 crore a year at a 10% cost of capital, a twentieth of what a full price match would cost.
The rival's price is below its cost on low-density routes, so its offer is unlikely to survive beyond its current funding.
hints: Sequence the structure from diagnosis to action rather than starting with responses.
First level: How serious and lasting is the threat, What is at stake for the client, Response options and payoffs.
What is at stake for the client: contribution at risk (volume likely to switch by segment, contribution lost per parcel switched) and knock-on cost from lower density on shared routes.

keyMetrics.name: Contribution at risk
keyMetrics.formula: parcels likely to switch x contribution per parcel

keyMetrics.name: Cost of faster remittance
keyMetrics.formula: daily COD collections x days of remittance brought forward x annual cost of capital

commonMistakes: Matching price across all D2C brands immediately, which destroys more contribution than the rival could take.
Treating the rival as permanent without testing whether its price covers its cost and how long its funding lasts.

frameworkPick.why: A competitor's move triggered the question, so the structure must assess the rival's staying power, the client's exposure and both price and non-price responses.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: Price is one response lever, but setting price in isolation ignores the rival's sustainability and non-price options.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: There is no broad profit decline to diagnose yet; the issue is a specific competitive threat.
distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The rival is the one entering; the client is not deciding whether to enter anything.

cases.title: Buying a Southeast Asian freight forwarder
cases.prompt: Our client is a European freight forwarding group with €6 billion of revenue, strong on Europe-Asia ocean and air freight. It is considering buying a Singapore-headquartered forwarder with €900 million revenue and €45 million EBITDA, mostly intra-Asia business. The seller is asking €650 million. Should the client buy it?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Build an intra-Asia presence; the board wants the deal earnings-accretive by year three and returning more than 9% on capital by year five.
Q: What are the target's real earnings? A: Gross profit (revenue less freight bought from carriers) is about €220 million, so EBITDA is about 20% of gross profit against the client's 30%.
Q: Is €45 million a normal year? A: Yes; EBITDA was about €90 million at the 2022 freight rate peak.
Q: Customers? A: Top 10 customers are 35% of gross profit, mostly electronics and apparel shippers moving production across Vietnam, India and Indonesia.

modelTree.label: Should the client buy the Singapore forwarder for €650 million?

children.label: Sell Europe-Asia lanes to target's Asian shippers
Sell intra-Asia lanes to client's European customers
Overlapping offices, IT and back office
Price vs standalone value plus synergies
Multiple paid (~14x EBITDA) vs comparable deals
Share of synergies paid to the seller
Key sales staff and customer attrition

hypotheses: At 30% conversion on €220 million gross profit (EBITDA ~€66 million) the price falls to about 10x, so the deal only works if the client can lift the target's conversion ratio to its own.
Procurement synergies of 2-3% on the target's ~€680 million of bought-in freight (€14-20 million a year) are more bankable than cross-selling.
Forwarding relationships sit with sales staff, so losing key people in Vietnam and India could erode a large part of the 35% top-10 gross profit.
hints: Use the standard acquisition logic: build up what the deal is worth in layers, then compare it with what is paid.
First level: Standalone value of the target, Synergies, Price and integration.
Synergies: revenue (sell Europe-Asia lanes to the target's shippers, sell intra-Asia lanes to the client's customers) and cost (carrier procurement, overlapping offices and IT).

keyMetrics.name: Conversion ratio
keyMetrics.formula: EBITDA / gross profit

keyMetrics.name: EV/EBITDA paid
keyMetrics.formula: price / normalised EBITDA = 650 / 45 ≈ 14.4x

commonMistakes: Valuing the target on revenue, most of which is pass-through freight cost, instead of gross profit.
Using peak-cycle earnings (2022) to justify the price, or ignoring where freight rates are in the cycle.

frameworkPick.why: A strategic buyer is evaluating a specific target at a specific price, so standalone value, synergies, price and integration are the right structure.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The client could enter intra-Asia organically, but the question is whether this particular deal at €650 million creates value.
distractorWhyNot.pe-dd: A financial sponsor's diligence focuses on standalone returns and exit; here synergies and integration with an existing group are central.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Growth in Asia is the motive, but the decision asked is a specific acquisition and its price.

cases.title: Launching an open parcel locker network
cases.prompt: A German parcel carrier with about 18% of the domestic B2C parcel market is considering launching 10,000 parcel lockers that any carrier, including rivals, could use for a fee. Each locker costs about €15,000 installed. How should it decide whether and how to launch?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Lower last-mile cost and win share, with the network breaking even within five years.
Q: What does a locker save? A: The client estimates that delivering to a locker costs about €0.60 per parcel against about €1.80 at the doorstep.

Q: Will consumers use them? A: Surveys suggest about 40% of urban online shoppers would use a locker within about 300 metres of home; on that basis the client expects about 9 of its own parcels per locker per day at planned sites.
Q: Who else runs lockers? A: The market leader runs a much larger network, almost all of it reserved for its own parcels; a few start-ups and retailers run open lockers in some cities.

modelTree.label: Should the carrier launch a 10,000-locker open network, and how?

children.label: Shoppers within ~300 m of a locker
Rival carriers (fee vs their doorstep cost)
Market leader's closed network (coverage, likely response)
Third-party parcels per locker per day

hypotheses: A locker costs about €5,500 a year (€3,000 depreciation over five years plus rent and upkeep), so at roughly €1 a parcel it breaks even near 15 parcels a day; the client's own 9 parcels at a €1.20 saving earn only about €3,900, so each locker needs about 5-6 third-party parcels a day at a net fee near €0.80.

Rival carriers will be reluctant to hand parcels to a competitor's network, so third-party uptake decides the case and may need a neutral brand, a partner or a retailer anchor; without it only the densest urban sites should be built.
hints: Cover the decision from the outside in: the market for the service first, then what exactly to launch, then whether it pays.
First level: Demand, Competing locker networks, Proposition and rollout, Economics.
Proposition and rollout: network rollout (site types, phasing by density), the fee charged to other carriers, and extra services (returns drop-off, app integration).

keyMetrics.name: Break-even parcels per locker per day
keyMetrics.formula: annual cost per locker / (365 x contribution per parcel)

keyMetrics.name: Locker utilisation
keyMetrics.formula: parcels deposited per day / compartments per locker

commonMistakes: Treating all 10,000 sites alike, when economics depend on density and the rollout must be phased by parcels per site.
Counting third-party fee income as certain without testing whether rival carriers will use a competitor-owned network.

frameworkPick.why: The carrier is deciding whether and how to launch a new offering in its existing market, which needs demand, competition, proposition design and launch economics.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The carrier already operates in German parcels; this is a new product in a market it is in, not entry into a new market.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: The fee to other carriers is one design choice inside the launch decision.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Lockers cut delivery cost, but the decision also turns on adoption, rivals' uptake and a €150 million investment, not just process efficiency.

cases.title: PE diligence on a freight marketplace
cases.prompt: A PE fund is considering investing ₹300 crore in an Indian digital freight marketplace that matches shippers with truck owners. It handled ₹1,200 crore of freight last year (GMV), up 60%, keeps a 6% take rate and loses about ₹60 crore a year. The founders want a ₹1,500 crore pre-money valuation. Should the fund invest?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does the fund need? A: 3x its money in five years, through a minority stake with a board seat.

Q: Where is growth coming from? A: One large cement company is now 35% of GMV, up from 10% a year ago; its lanes earn about a 1% take rate because the platform guaranteed fixed rates and absorbs spot price swings. The rest of GMV earns about 8.7%.
Q: How do payments work? A: The platform pays truckers within about 3 days but collects from shippers in about 60 days, so working capital grows with GMV.
Q: The market? A: Indian road freight is worth well over ₹10 lakh crore a year and highly fragmented; digital brokers handle a low single-digit share.

modelTree.label: Should the fund invest ₹300 crore at ₹1,500 crore pre-money for 3x?

children.label: Shipper freight open to brokers (spot and contract FTL)
Digital brokers' share and its growth
Sustainable take rates vs offline brokers
Working capital intensity (pay fast, collect slow)
Quality of growth and unit economics
Anchor cement client (35% of GMV, ~1% take)
Rest of GMV (~8.7% take), by client cohort
Take rate net of rate guarantees
Variable costs (payments, trip support, bad debt)
Fixed costs and path to breakeven
Reprice or exit the anchor contract
Entry price (~21x net revenue) vs comparables
Exit routes and value needed for 3x

hypotheses: Excluding the anchor client, GMV grew only about 16% (from ~₹675 crore to ~₹780 crore), not 60%, so the growth story is largely one low-margin contract.

Contribution on the anchor's lanes is negative once payment costs and rate guarantees are counted, and its 60-day receivables tie up a large share of the ~₹190 crore of working capital, so it deepens losses rather than reducing them.

A 3x return needs an exit equity value of about ₹5,400 crore for a 16.7% stake, roughly ₹540 crore of net revenue at 10x, which means ~50% annual growth in net revenue that the non-anchor book is not showing.
hints: Use a PE diligence structure, and test the headline growth number before trusting it.
First level: Market attractiveness, Quality of growth and unit economics, Value creation and exit.

Market attractiveness: addressable freight spend (shipper freight open to brokers, digital brokers' share) and the structural economics of brokerage (sustainable take rates, working capital intensity).

keyMetrics.name: Take rate
keyMetrics.formula: net revenue / GMV

keyMetrics.name: Working capital
keyMetrics.formula: GMV / 365 x (receivable days - payable days)

keyMetrics.name: Exit value needed
keyMetrics.formula: investment x target multiple / ownership share = 300 x 3 / (300 / 1,800)

commonMistakes: Accepting the headline 60% GMV growth without splitting it by client and take rate.
Ignoring working capital, which grows with GMV and can absorb much of the ₹300 crore before any growth is funded.

frameworkPick.why: A financial investor deciding on price and return needs a diligence structure (market, target, value creation, exit), and the twist is that growth comes from a loss-making contract, so unit economics and profitability analysis sit at the centre.

distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: The market is clearly large; sizing it does not answer whether this target at this price can return 3x.
distractorWhyNot.ma: This is a minority financial investment with no synergies or integration, so a strategic acquisition frame does not fit.

cases.title: Express carrier loses its anchor client
cases.prompt: Our client is a mid-sized Indian express parcel company that had revenue of about ₹1,100 crore a year, roughly at breakeven, until its largest marketplace client, 35% of volume, moved deliveries in-house over the past six months. The company now loses about ₹13 crore a month and has roughly nine months of cash. Lenders want cost cuts and asset sales; the founders want to keep the national network to win new clients. What should it do?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does the cost base look like? A: Variable costs (riders paid per drop, trucks hired per trip, packaging) run at about 60% of revenue. Semi-fixed costs are about ₹37 crore a month: 30 hubs and 900 delivery centres on lease, owned sorters, about 150 owned line haul trucks and staff.
Q: Where was the lost volume? A: Concentrated in Tier-2/3 towns in the North and East; metro volume is mainly D2C brands and smaller marketplaces and is stable and profitable at contribution level.
Q: What cash sources exist? A: Two owned automated sortation hubs (book value about ₹140 crore); at any time the company also holds about ₹90 crore of COD cash owed to clients, remitted on D+5.
Q: Any hard constraints? A: Lender covenants require a credible plan to reach monthly EBITDA breakeven within nine months.

modelTree.label: How can the client stop a ₹13 crore monthly loss within nine months?

children.label: Collect overdue receivables from B2B and D2C clients
Renegotiate lease and vendor payment terms
Sale and leaseback of the two sortation hubs
Resize the network to remaining volume
Merge underloaded centres in towns the anchor left
Hand thin pin codes to franchise partners
Cut or merge lanes built for anchor volume
Replace owned trucks with per-trip hire

hypotheses: Losing 35% of volume removed about ₹32 crore of monthly revenue but only about ₹19 crore of variable cost, leaving ₹13 crore of semi-fixed cost uncovered; breakeven needs about a third of the ₹37 crore semi-fixed base, mostly Tier-2/3 centres and lanes built for the anchor, to go or turn variable, and franchising thin pin codes does that while keeping the national coverage the founders want.
A sale and leaseback of the two hubs near book value (about ₹140 crore, against perhaps ₹1-1.5 crore a month of new rent) roughly doubles the nine-month runway without touching client COD cash.

Rebuilding volume alone would need about ₹33 crore a month of new revenue at a 40% contribution margin (₹13 crore / 0.4), close to the whole lost anchor, so new clients can close only part of the gap within nine months and cost resizing must do most of the work.
hints: Order the structure by time horizon, from what must happen this quarter to what pays off next year.
First level: Secure the cash runway, Resize the network to remaining volume, Rebuild profitable volume.

Secure the cash runway: release working capital (collect overdue receivables, renegotiate lease and vendor terms) and raise cash (sale and leaseback of the sortation hubs, bridge funding from investors).

keyMetrics.name: Monthly cash burn
keyMetrics.formula: EBITDA loss + capex + increase in working capital

keyMetrics.name: Break-even volume
keyMetrics.formula: monthly semi-fixed costs / contribution per parcel

commonMistakes: Funding losses by delaying COD remittance: that cash belongs to clients, and holding it risks contract breaches and losing the D2C clients the recovery depends on.
Cutting (or protecting) the whole network uniformly instead of separating profitable metro operations from Tier-2/3 capacity built for the lost client.

frameworkPick.why: A loss-making firm with nine months of cash needs a turnaround structure (runway, cost reset, revenue rebuild), and most of the fix is an operational redesign of the network around the remaining volume.

distractorWhyNot.growth: Chasing new volume first ignores the nine-month runway and a cost base sized for volume that has gone.
distractorWhyNot.competitive-response: The loss is a client insourcing, not a rival's move to counter; the issue is survival and resizing.

cases.title: Fixing loss-making small online sellers
cases.prompt: Our client, a large Indian express parcel carrier, serves about 40,000 small and medium online sellers through a self-serve platform. The segment brings in ₹600 crore of revenue but loses about ₹15 crore at contribution level. Management assumes the smallest sellers are the problem and plans a minimum monthly fee. How should the client segment these sellers and decide what to do?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Make the segment contribution-positive within a year without losing more than 10% of its revenue.

Q: What does the data show? A: Loss-making sellers are spread across all sizes. Sellers with RTO above 25%, mostly COD-heavy fashion and impulse categories, bring about ₹200 crore of revenue and lose about ₹20 crore; the rest earn about ₹5 crore.

Q: How are they priced? A: One rate card by weight and zone. High-RTO sellers dispatch about 2.5 crore parcels a year at an average 40% RTO, paying about ₹62 of forward freight per parcel plus about ₹43 per RTO (70% of forward). A delivered parcel costs about ₹58 to serve; an RTO parcel costs about ₹130 all-in, counting failed attempts and the reverse leg.
Q: Competition? A: Shipping aggregators resell several carriers to small sellers and route each order to the cheapest option.

modelTree.label: How should the client segment 40,000 sellers to turn a ₹15 crore loss positive?

children.label: Yield per parcel (zone and weight mix)
High-RTO sellers (>25% RTO; ~₹200 crore revenue, -₹20 crore)
Causes (impulse COD, fake orders, bad addresses)
Share fixable with tools vs inherent
RTO billed at the full forward rate or RTO-linked tiers
Minimum fee only where pickup density is low

hypotheses: RTO, not seller size, drives the loss: high-RTO sellers are a third of revenue and lose about ₹20 crore while the rest earn about ₹5 crore, so a minimum fee on small sellers hits profitable or marginal accounts and misses the cause.

Billing RTO at the full forward rate (₹62 instead of ₹43) adds about ₹19 on each of roughly 1 crore RTO parcels, about ₹19 crore, enough on its own to make the segment positive; it raises high-RTO sellers' bills by under 10%, whereas billing RTO at its full ₹130 cost would raise them about 44% and push them to rivals through aggregators.

Cutting high-RTO sellers' RTO from 40% to 30% with COD-to-prepaid nudges and order verification gains about ₹29 on each parcel converted at today's prices (₹72 of cost saved less ₹43 of RTO fee forgone), about ₹7 crore, a buffer if the least fixable sellers leave within the ₹60 crore revenue limit.
hints: Let the economics choose the segmentation variable rather than the one management assumed, then act segment by segment.
First level: Variables that drive seller profitability, Profile and size each segment, Strategy by segment.

Variables that drive seller profitability: cost-to-serve drivers (RTO rate by COD share and category, pickup density) and revenue drivers (monthly volume, yield by zone and weight, weight under-declaration).

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per parcel by segment
keyMetrics.formula: per dispatched parcel: forward freight + RTO rate x RTO charge - (1 - RTO rate) x cost per delivered parcel - RTO rate x all-in cost per RTO parcel

keyMetrics.name: RTO rate
keyMetrics.formula: parcels returned to origin / parcels dispatched

commonMistakes: Accepting management's size-based hypothesis without testing it against the data, which shows RTO is the driver.
Segmenting by descriptive traits such as city or seller age that do not map to cost-to-serve.

frameworkPick.why: The core task is finding the segmentation that explains losses (RTO behaviour, not size), and the main fix is differentiated pricing by segment, so the two frameworks combine.

distractorWhyNot.operations: RTO-reduction tools are one lever inside the segment strategy; the question is which sellers to treat differently and on what terms.
distractorWhyNot.growth: The goal is profit, with revenue loss only a constraint; growing the segment as it stands would deepen losses.

chainDrills.prompt: An express carrier pays diesel and tolls for 32-ft trucks running overnight between its Delhi and Mumbai hubs. Which stage does this cost belong to?
chainDrills.why: Moving consolidated loads between hubs is line haul; first mile and last mile cover moves to and from customers, and the hub stage covers sorting, not transport.

chainDrills.prompt: Put the stages of the logistics value chain in order, from winning a shipper's business to settling what happens after delivery.
chainDrills.why: A shipper is signed and the shipment booked, the parcel is picked up, sorted at the origin hub, moved by line haul, delivered at the last mile, and finally returns, COD remittance and claims are settled.

chainDrills.prompt: Pickups are on time and line haul trucks leave on schedule, but each truck carries only about 60% of the day's parcels; the rest wait for the next day's truck because sorting finishes after departure. Where is the problem?
chainDrills.why: Parcels arrive on time and trucks depart on time, so pickup and line haul are working; the bottleneck is hub sorting capacity, which misses the truck cut-off.

chainDrills.prompt: Assign each item to the value chain stage it belongs to.

items.item: Rate card discount negotiated with a D2C brand
Bike fuel allowance for staff collecting parcels from sellers' premises
Rent for an automated sortation centre
Hire charges for a spot-market truck between two hubs
Per-drop pay to a delivery rider
Compensation paid to a shipper for a parcel lost in transit

chainDrills.why: The tricky ones: the fuel allowance is first mile, not last mile, because it is for collecting from sellers; the lost-parcel compensation sits in claims (s6) even though the loss happened earlier in the chain, because settling claims is a post-delivery activity; the discount is a pricing decision made at booking, even though it shows up as lower revenue on every parcel.

chainDrills.prompt: RTO cost per parcel has doubled for one D2C client. Riders at the same delivery centres show unchanged first-attempt success on other clients, but 40% of this client's failed attempts are coded 'address incomplete or pin code mismatch'. Its orders flow from its website into the carrier's system through an API set up last quarter. Which stage caused the rise?
chainDrills.why: The cost shows up in returns (s6) and the failures happen at the last mile (s5), but riders perform normally on other clients. The bad addresses enter at booking and integration, where an API with no address or pin-code validation lets undeliverable orders through, so the fix (validation at order capture) sits in s1. First-mile pickup only collects and weighs parcels.

chainDrills.prompt: An express carrier's cash fell by about ₹70 crore in a quarter while revenue, EBITDA and receivables were all steady. COD collections run at about ₹14 crore a day, riders still deposit collected cash the same day, and no shipper contract terms have changed. Which stage explains the cash fall?
chainDrills.why: ₹70 crore is five days of COD collections (5 x ₹14 crore), so remittances are going out about five days sooner, for example a new payout run paying shippers at D+2 when contracts allow D+7, which shrinks the float the carrier holds. Collection by riders (s5) and contract terms (s1) are unchanged; remittance to shippers sits in s6.
